L37: Beyond the Event Horizon of Keccak, Extending the Observation from 2011 and applications
L38: 
L39: Danilo Gligoroski
L40: 
L41: Show abstract
L42: 
L43: 【19†Attacks and cryptanalysis】
L44: In 2011 we observed that a single path in the Keccak sponge from a state whose capacity has all zero bits back to such a state yields an explicit, infinite family of second preimages for every message of at least one full rate block. Finding such a path costs about 2^(c/2), which lies "beyond the event horizon" for SHA3-256 (c=512). In this paper we give three novel theorems around that observation.
L45: First, the capacity can have any value x: a two-block meet-in-the-middle loop from x back to x, found at heuristic cost about 2*2^(c/2), gives the same unlimited family of second preimages requiring no further search, with connectors to and from x at about the same cost again (Theorem 1). Theorem 2 extends this to k-block loops and to cycles of the capacity map.
L46: A single-state bridge, a state S with cap(f(S)) = cap(f^-1(S)), where cap denotes the capacity part of the state, also gives such a family but costs about 2^c. Theorem 3 gives cheap collisions and a bridge-amplified multicollision: one inner collision and one connector yield equal-length Joux-style 2^k-multicollisions for every k, instead of Joux's k collision searches; to our knowledge this is the first such construction for generic sponges with search cost independent of k.
L47: We give verified full-round examples on Keccak-f[200] and on Keccak-f[1600] with c=32. The second part of the paper offers novel protocols built on the asymmetry between minting and forging Keccak bridges. They include proof of work with hardness-adaptive capacity, dual-capacity commitments anchored by the real SHA3-256 digest, bridges as zero-knowledge-committed tokens, and a self-enforcing bounty market for reduced-round security.
L48: To our knowledge, these are the first unkeyed Keccak-based protocols that deliberately set the capacity so that the generic bridge cost is a feasible, tunable hardness parameter. We prove the three theorems, machine-check the stated algebraic results in Lean 4, and provide reproducible experiments and open-source proof-of-concept code. The applications are design proposals whose end-to-end security remains open.

L53: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models
L54: 
L55: Sikhar Patranabis
L56: 
L57: Show abstract
L58: 
L59: 【22†Foundations】
L60: Identity-based encryption (IBE) is required to support a superpolynomial-size identity space using only polynomial-size public parameters. This compression requirement underlies known barriers to IBE in the generic (pairing-free) group model. Cryptographic group actions, motivated prominently by isogeny-based cryptography, support many advanced primitives beyond public-key encryption. However, no generic construction of IBE from the basic group-action interface is known.
L61: Existing generic-group barriers do not resolve this question as they do not translate to generic group-action models. We establish the first tight barriers to IBE in two variants of the generic group-action model. In the type-safe generic group-action model, we prove that an IBE scheme with negligible correctness error and $n$ non-origin action-set element-handles in its public parameters can support at most $n$ identities, even for a weak notion of fully selective security.
L62: We show that this bound holds irrespective of the number of action-set element-handles in identity secret keys. We further establish that this bound is tight by demonstrating a matching construction.
L63: We then extend this tight characterization to a natural class of IBE schemes in the random-representation generic group-action model (including against representation-sensitive adversaries) under conditions ensuring that identity keys retain no hidden action-set encodings and discarded private encodings leave no residual information. We give a natural syntactic condition for the latter property.
L64: For actions additionally equipped with an inversion-like twist, we obtain a more general upper bound (including the same tight bound for odd-order actions). Our results provide the first formal evidence that IBE is likely to require additional algebraic structure or non-black-box techniques beyond the generic group-action interface. More broadly, we provide a new framework for proving lower bounds in generic group-action models.

L69: PIR through the Lens of Probabilistic Inference
L70: 
L71: Dana Dachman-Soled
L72: 
L73: Show abstract
L74: 
L75: 【22†Foundations】
L76: Private Information Retrieval (PIR) allows a client to retrieve an entry of a database while revealing no information about the requested index to the servers. Classic information-theoretic PIR protocols of Chor et al. (FOCS '95, JACM '98) and Ambainis (ICALP '97) achieve sublinear client computation and communication complexity with a constant number of servers, but require each server to perform computation linear in the database size.
L77: In this work, we ask for which classes of structured databases the server computation can be substantially reduced while preserving the communication complexity and privacy guarantees of these protocols. Our main contribution is a new connection between server computation in information-theoretic PIR and probabilistic inference. We show that the computation performed by every server in both the Chor et al.
L78: protocol and the recursive protocol of Ambainis can be viewed as computing a marginal probability of a product distribution. Consequently, efficient exact probabilistic inference algorithm immediately yields a faster server algorithm for PIR. We formalize this connection through the notion of inference complexity, which captures the complexity of evaluating these marginals.
L79: Using this framework, we obtain improved server computation for several broad classes of functions, including read-once arithmetic formulas, graphical models of bounded treewidth (and consequently arithmetic circuits of bounded treewidth), functions with low communication complexity, and functions with sparse Fourier representations.
L80: The resulting protocols preserve the communication complexity, client computation, and number of servers of the underlying PIR constructions while substantially reducing server computation for these structured function classes. Finally, we complement our algorithms with conditional lower bounds.
L81: Assuming the randomized Circuit Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (rCSETH), we show that, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a constant \(c\) such that no uniform algorithm can compute the first (virtual) server's response in the Chor et al. or Ambainis protocol on all \(n\)-input Boolean circuits of size at most \(n^c\) in time \(O(N^{1-\varepsilon})\), where \(N=2^n\).
L82: Thus, under rCSETH, substantially sublinear server computation cannot be achieved uniformly for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits.

L87: An Algebraic Polynomial Evaluation Datastructure for Fields of Large Characteristic
L88: 
L89: Hiroki Okada, Rachel Player, and Simon Pohmann
L90: 
L91: Show abstract
L92: 
L93: 【22†Foundations】
L94: In this work, we study (multivariate) polynomial evaluation datastructures, i.e. algorithms that can evaluate a multivariate polynomial at any input point, using random access to some precomputed encoding of the polynomial. Multiple constructions have been proposed in the literature, with the work by Bhargava, Ghosh, Guo, Kumar and Umans (2024) achieving optimal datastructure size and query complexity, up to polynomial factors.
L95: For $n \in d^{o(1)}$ this is equivalent to having datastructure size $d^{n + o(n)} (d n \log q)^{O(1)}$ and query complexity $(d n \log q)^{O(1)}$ for an $n$-variate polynomial of total degree $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. However, the algorithm of Bhargava et al. is not algebraic, since it requires lifting prime field elements to $\mathbb{Z}$.
L96: An algebraic algorithm would be desirable, as an algebraic model of computation is natural for studying polynomial evaluation and is the standard model in algebraic complexity theory. One approach to finding algebraic polynomial evaluation datastructures is to use univariate polynomial interpolation to reconstruct the polynomial along algebraic curves.
L97: This approach was first made explicit by Bhargava, Ghosh, Kumar and Mohapatra (2023), who used it to build an essentially optimal algebraic polynomial evaluation datastructure for fields of small characteristic $p = \mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F}_q) \in d^{o(1)}$. Over these fields, their construction refutes a previous conjecture by Miltersen. For fields of larger characteristic, it remains an open problem to find an algebraic algorithm with optimal datastructure size and query complexity.
L98: In this work, we propose a new way to construct algebraic curves over prime fields that allow polynomial interpolation: by deriving curves from the base-$\beta$ representation of (lifts of) prime field elements, we are able to recursively reduce the evaluation problem to points in boxes of decreasing size. This leads to a datastructure whose performance scales much more favourably with $p$.
L99: Concretely, we improve the dependency of the query complexity on $p$ from $p^{O(1)}$ to $d^{2\log_2 \ln\ln p} \ln p$, and completely remove the dependency on $p$ from the datastructure size. Its query complexity is still slightly super-polynomial in $d \log p$. Nevertheless, a variant of our results is enough to disprove Miltersen's conjecture for all finite fields, including prime fields.
L100: We further show that for a certain class of datastructures, which captures natural generalizations of our approach, the query complexity is lower-bounded by $d^{(1 - o(1))\log_3\ln\ln p}$. Consequently, within this class, our construction is optimal up to a constant in the exponent.

L105: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms
L106: 
L107: Diego F. Aranha and Paulo L. Barreto
L108: 
L109: Show abstract
L110: 
L111: 【29†Implementation】
L112: We revisit scalar multiplication on prime curves $y^2 = x^3 + b$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the family including secp256k1, BN, and BLS curves. We apply a 15-year-old technique in a novel way to improve the best complete addition from $12$ to $11$ multiplications (or $10$ for mixed coordinates) for the first time in 10 years: its final stage is a 3D cross product, which needs only five multiplications.
L113: We implement the new formulas on the \texttt{libsecp256k1} library, with an improvement of $5.2$\% in constant-time fixed-base scalar multiplication. Furthermore, we propose a complete tripling formula with the same cost as incomplete tripling in Jacobian coordinates, and combine both formulas into an exception-free width-3 $\tau$-NAF with $\tau = 1 - \omega$ and a six-point precomputed table.
L114: In an operation-count model it is about 14\% faster than exception-free GLV-based scalar multiplication at 256 bits and 3--7\% faster than the fastest incomplete GLV.
L115: A constant-time implementation in RELIC confirms the model on the BLS families: in $\mathbb{G}_1$ of BLS12-381, BLS24-509 and BLS48-575 the $\tau$-NAF is 9--13\% faster than GLV with the same complete formulas, and the regular variant is 10--12\% faster than regular GLV with complete formulas and 5--9\% faster than regular GLV with incomplete Jacobian formulas.
L116: In $\mathbb{G}_2$ of the same curves, where GLS gives the baseline, the $\tau$-NAF stays 10--11\% faster than GLS with complete formulas and 7--9\% faster with Jacobian formulas, while the regular variant gains at most 6\%. We also develop an `imaginary' version of Toom-Cook that is useful for the $\mathbb{G}_T$ extension field arithmetic, yielding a 4--6\% improvement in $\mathbb{G}_T$ exponentiation for BLS24-509 and BLS48-575.
L117: A cyclotomic cube at 0.77 multiplications carries the $\tau$-adic method over to $\mathbb{G}_T$, where it makes exponentiation 3\% faster on BLS24-509 and 11\% faster on BLS48-575.

L122: Efficient SIMD SHAKE through Cost-Aware Permutation Scheduling
L123: 
L124: Hang Zhang, Ya Shi, Ying Liu, and Xianhui Lu
L125: 
L126: Show abstract
L127: 
L128: 【29†Implementation】
L129: Lattice-based cryptography uses SHAKE to expand seeds into byte strings for matrix generation and sampling. SIMD Keccak implementations process multiple hash streams in parallel. Differences in stream lengths and input dependencies can prevent full SIMD utilization. We present a cost-aware method for scheduling Keccak permutations across hash streams during a single execution of a cryptographic algorithm. The method groups ready streams and divides long streams into segments for regrouping.
L130: A model of permutation calls, state movement, initialization, and input preparation guides the selection of stream groups, segment lengths, and state placements. We evaluate ML-KEM and HAETAE on an Apple M5, a Cortex-A72, and an Intel Core i5-11500, using Keccak kernels that process two, four, or eight streams per call. ML-KEM achieves speedups of up to $1.31\times$ for encapsulation and $1.44\times$ for decapsulation, while HAETAE achieves up to $1.28\times$ for signing and $1.26\times$ for verification.

L135: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days
L136: 
L137: Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi, Victor Hertz, Hugo Jacinto, Larissa Kroell, André Schrottenloher, Peter Shanahan, Élie Gouzien, Rémi de La Vieuville, and Vivien Londe
L138: 
L139: Show abstract
L140: 
L141: 【19†Attacks and cryptanalysis】
L142: We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. After proposing a comprehensive view of the modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, we make explicit their logical circuits and the trade-offs they enable.
L143: We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one based on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat-qubit architectures. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat-qubit architectures the adder from Gidney’s 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048.
L144: We combine our adder compilation and a coarser resource estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these compilations lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048.
L145: Assuming a 1$\mu$s error-correction cycle time, a 10$\mu$s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the operations compiled for RSA-2048, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6\,700 cat qubits and 21~minutes.
L146: Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The requirement on no bit-flips (which corresponds to a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by using an additional concatenation layer into a distance-3 bit-flip error-correcting code. In that case, we estimate that the cost of RSA-2048 increases to about 45 000 cat qubits.

L151: Rerandomizable Garbling Beyond BHHO-KMHE and a Construction from LWE
L152: 
L153: Raphael Heitjohann, Jonas von der Heyden, and Tibor Jager
L154: 
L155: Show abstract
L156: 
L157: 【36†Cryptographic protocols】
L158: Rerandomizable garbling schemes (RGS) are a fundamental primitive enabling advanced cryptographic constructions such as multi-hop homomorphic encryption (Gentry, Halevi, Vaikuntanathan, CRYPTO 2010), iO-combiners (Ananth, Jain, Naor, Sahai, Yogev, CRYPTO 2016), and YOSO-style MPC (Acharya, Hazay, Kolesnikov, Prabhakaran, TCC 2022 and CRYPTO 2024).
L159: All known RGS instantiations rely on discrete-logarithm-type assumptions, concretely via the BHHO scheme (Boneh, Halevi, Hamburg, Ostrovsky, CRYPTO 2008) and its recent pairing-based variant (Heitjohann, von der Heyden, Jager, CRYPTO 2025).
L160: This reliance stems from the use of key-and-message homomorphic encryption (KMHE) that supports rerandomization and strong "key-privacy under leakage", which hides the applied homomorphic transformations and is currently only achievable using BHHO-style bitwise encryption in combination with permutation-based homomorphisms. Our first main contribution is a new garbling technique that shifts the burden of hiding homomorphic transformations from the encryption scheme to the garbling itself.
L161: This allows us to construct RGS from KMHE schemes with substantially weaker properties, avoiding the need for bitwise encryption and permutation-based homomorphisms, and enabling the construction of RGS from KMHE with other homomorphisms, such as additively-homomorphic ones. As a second contribution, we give a concrete lattice-based instantiation of the required KMHE primitive, based on LWE.
L162: This construction is a variant of the GSW FHE scheme (Gentry, Sahai, Waters, CRYPTO 2013), which uses new techniques for rerandomization and is tailored to the requirements of our new garbling scheme by supporting a "homomorphic"/"lossy" mode. This yields the first RGS construction that does not rely on discrete-logarithm assumptions and may provide post-quantum security.

L167: Quantum Multi-Collision Lower Bounds for Arbitrary Bounded Types
L168: 
L169: Tianci Peng, Shiqi Hou, and Xiaoyang Dong
L170: 
L171: Show abstract
L172: 
L173: 【22†Foundations】
L174: We study quantum collision finding for functions of prescribed exact type. For fixed constants $k\ge r\ge2$ and $N=kn$, consider functions $f:[N]\to\mathbb Z_q$ of type $(k^n)$, with exactly $n$ distinct output values and $k$ preimages for each value. We prove that the worst-case bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding $r$-collisions in $\ell$ distinct equality classes is \[ \Theta_{k,r}\!\left( \ell^{\,2^{r-1}/(2^r-1)} N^{(2^{r-1}-1)/(2^r-1)} \right) \] for $1\le\ell\le N^{2^{-r}}$.
L175: The result is uniform over all feasible alphabet sizes $q\ge n$. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle (CPO). We establish a recurrence for intermediate collision counts and control its accumulated error to obtain database tails exponentially small in $\ell$. The improved CPO soundness estimate then converts these database bounds into function-query lower bounds.
L176: Moreover, we extend the analysis to arbitrary exact types with bounded class sizes, without requiring any particular class size to occur linearly often. The resulting lower bounds are tight when forward permutation access is additionally available, although they need not be tight for the original function-query problem. Finally, a sampling reduction relates our collision bounds to sparse $k$-distinctness instances.
L177: A separate analysis using Belovs's transfer framework recovers the same lower-bound exponent, establishing a concrete connection between the two approaches.

L182: Tractable, Not Truncated: Colored-Noise TRNG Security via Fractional Brownian Motion
L183: 
L184: Maciej Skórski, Nathalie Bochard, and Licinius Benea
L185: 
L186: Show abstract
L187: 
L188: 【22†Foundations】
L189: Oscillator-based true random number generators derive randomness from timing fluctuations driven by thermal and flicker noise, and flicker gains weight as technology advances and transistors shrink. Its long memory leaks information about past, which existing models either discard or truncate, overstating security. We introduce a rigorous and tractable framework for colored noise, including the white and flicker noise of oscillators.
L190: We model the oscillator phase by fractional Brownian motion and prove a quasi-renewal property: the phase uncertainty left after conditioning on the entire past depends only on the elapsed time. This yields closed-form worst-case min-entropy and sampling requirements. We also extend spectral and Allan-variance analysis to finite samples, so the noise parameters are estimated consistently from a single timing trace.
L191: The pipeline from measurement to sampling requirement is closed-form and needs no simulation. Experiments across FPGA and ASIC platforms show that flicker dominates: its variance meets white noise within about 100 cycles and accounts for more than 99% of uncertainty behind the targeted 0.99 min-entropy rate. Methods relying exclusively on thermal noise require adjustment or redesign: incorporating flicker noise enables a two-to-three orders of magnitude increase in bitrate.

L196: Radical isogenies on every model
L197: 
L198: Thomas Decru
L199: 
L200: Show abstract
L201: 
L202: 【43†Public-key cryptography】
L203: Radical isogeny formulae compute a cyclic chain of $N$-isogenies with one $N$th root per step and without sampling torsion points, but for general $N$ they were only known in Tate normal form. We give radical steps of every odd degree $N$ directly on short Weierstrass, Montgomery, twisted Edwards, Huff, extended Jacobi quartic, twisted Hessian, Legendre and Jacobi intersection curves, on Kummer lines, and on all curves with a rational point of order~$2$. Our approach is model-independent.
L204: The Tate normal form data is obtained from the $x$-coordinate of the kernel generator by a shifted recursion, and the codomain is recovered in the original model by locating the image of a distinguished torsion point, without square roots. In Tate normal form we lower the cost of a step from $12.5N$ to $10N$ multiplications plus one exponentiation, and short Weierstrass curves come close at $10N+35$. Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves cost $10.5N+O(1)$.
L205: However, pushing a point through their steps costs only $2N$ multiplications without precomputation, against $2N+16$ plus a shared $2N-7$ in Tate normal form, which makes them the cheapest models for chains that transport torsion points, e.g.\ for all $N\ge19$ when two points are pushed. The other models cost between $11.5N+O(\log N)$ and $15.5N+O(\log N)$ per step. All algorithms are inversion-free, with exact operation counts.

L210: Towards Quantum Sensing for Side-Channel Analysis
L211: 
L212: Oliver Butowski, Paul Haas, Jonas Hasenkrug, Niklas Mathes, Emanuele Strieder, Michael Kunzer, Jan Jeske, Nisha Jacob Kabakci, and Marc Stöttinger
L213: 
L214: Show abstract
L215: 
L216: 【46†Applications】
L217: Side-Channel Analysis is an established field of research to assess implementation vulnerabilities of cryptographic algorithms. One typically exploited side-channel is the electromagnetic (EM) near-field, which is proportional to the data-dependent currents flowing through an Integrated Circuit (IC). The field of Quantum Sensing (QS) based on Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers has shown promising approaches for different measurement configurations like scanning or spatially resolved wide-field imaging.
L218: Already today, QS has been used in the analysis of (quasi-)static magnetic fields on ICs in spatially-resolved wide-field magnetometers. In this work, we study the applicability of QS for the analysis of dynamic EM fields of ICs. For the first time, we demonstrate spectral-temporal analysis of the EM-side-channel using an NV-center-based Radio-Frequency spectrometer.
L219: Our sensor has a real-time bandwidth of 1.1 GHz with adjustable center frequency and directly probes the frequency spectrum via NV center interactions in the time domain. The approach circumvents any computations like Fourier transforms or performing frequency sweeps, enabling GHz-realtime bandwidths.
L220: We use this spectrometer to analyze the EM emanations of an RSA decryption and perform leakage detection of a software implementation of the Number Theoretic Transform - a building block of all current lattice based post-quantum algorithms - running on a Cortex M4 commercial off-the-shelf microcontroller.

L225: Alg\{Ossa\}: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery
L226: 
L227: Xiangyu Su, Yuma Tamagawa, Mario Larangeira, Zengpeng Li, and Keisuke Tanaka
L228: 
L229: Show abstract
L230: 
L231: 【36†Cryptographic protocols】
L232: Secure aggregation lets clients reveal only an aggregate of their private contributions, supporting a variety of applications, including privacy-preserving sensing, collaborative analytics, and federated learning. Building on the single-server, committee-aided model for one-shot clients used by OPA and Willow~(CRYPTO~'25), we present Ossa, a generic construction with a modular security analysis.
L233: Ossa realizes the standard secure aggregation functionality with non-selective abort against a malicious server, but leaves role selection unspecified and provides no delivery guarantee. We therefore present AlgOssa, which integrates Ossa into an Algorand-style consensus backbone in which cryptographic sortition selects fresh potential leaders and verifier committees in each round and refreshes the decryptor committee from finalized chain state at key epochs.
L234: AlgOssa further selects the server from among the potential leaders, and we establish an explicit lower bound on the probability that the selected server is honest. Consequently, the probability that a round delivers a non-empty aggregate is bounded below by a positive constant, yielding an eventual delivery guarantee across repeated rounds. This variable delivery cadence fits delay-tolerant statistical sensing and, with persistent buffering and staleness control, buffered asynchronous federated learning.
L235: Our generic core supports classical and post-quantum instantiation routes; we evaluate complete local classical rounds and demonstrate the feasibility of the post-quantum route.

L240: Unshuffling Fisher-Yates: Practical Recovery of Length-128 Permutations and Application to ML-DSA
L241: 
L242: Jonas Schupp, Anna Baumeister, Antonia Wachter-Zeh, and Georg Sigl
L243: 
L244: Show abstract
L245: 
L246: 【19†Attacks and cryptanalysis】
L247: Shuffling is a standard hiding countermeasure against (single-trace) side-channel attacks on the number-theoretic transform (NTT) of lattice-based post-quantum schemes, such as ML-DSA. The Fisher-Yates algorithm can be used to generate the underlying random permutation. Recovering this permutation itself from a single trace has so far only been studied for short sequences.
L248: We present a practical attack on a software implementation of Fisher-Yates for sequences of length 128, the number of butterfly operations in one layer of ML-DSA’s NTT. We identify the exploitable leakage of the algorithm, detect and remove the timing variations caused by rejection sampling and extract Hamming weight and identity leakage from a single trace per shuffle.
L249: We encode these hints as a constraint-programming problem with a soft objective function and enumerate the most likely permutations in order of descending likelihood. Applied to a shuffled ML-DSA-44 NTT, the recovered permutations are used to re-order the butterfly leakage, and recover the secret polynomial s1 either directly or up to a few coefficients that are enumerated directly.
L250: Protecting ML-DSA’s NTT with Fisher-Yates-based shuffling does, therefore, not, by itself, prevent side-channel-assisted key recovery.
